Zeros of Stern polynomials in the complex plane

David Altizio
Abstract

The classical Stern sequence of positive integers was extended to a polynomial sequence Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) by Klavžar et. al. by defining S0​(λ)=0S_{0}(\lambda)=0, S1​(λ)=1S_{1}(\lambda)=1, and

S2​n​(λ)=λ​Sn​(λ),S2​n+1​(λ)=Sn​(λ)+Sn+1​(λ).S_{2n}(\lambda)=\lambda S_{n}(\lambda),\quad S_{2n+1}(\lambda)=S_{n}(\lambda)+S_{n+1}(\lambda).

Dilcher et. al. conjectured that all roots of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) lie in the half-plane {Rew<1}\{\operatorname{Re}w<1\}. We make partial progress on this conjecture by proving that {|w−2|≤1}⊆ℂ\{|w-2|\leq 1\}\subseteq\mathbb{C} does not contain any roots of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda). Our proof uses the Parabola Theorem for convergence of complex continued fractions. As a corollary, we establish a conjecture of Ulas and Ulas by showing that Sp​(λ)S_{p}(\lambda) is irreducible in ℤ⁡[λ]\mathbb{Z}[\lambda] whenever pp is a positive prime.

1 Introduction

The Stern sequence (sn)n≥0(s_{n})_{n\geq 0} of positive integers, named after Moritz Abraham Stern, is given by s0=0s_{0}=0, s1=1s_{1}=1, and

s2​n=sn,s2​n+1=sn+sn+1.s_{2n}=s_{n},\quad s_{2n+1}=s_{n}+s_{n+1}. (1.1)

There is a vast body of literature (e.g. [2, 10, 12, 15] and the references therein) about the Stern sequence. Perhaps the most striking property of the Stern sequence is that every positive rational number appears exactly once in the sequence (sn+1/sn)n≥1(s_{n+1}/s_{n})_{n\geq 1}, giving an explicit enumeration of ℚ+\mathbb{Q}^{+}. Stern proved this fact 15 years before Cantor introduced the notion of a countable set!

In [8], Klavžar, Milutinović, and Petr define a polynomial analogue Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) of the Stern sequence via S0​(λ)=0S_{0}(\lambda)=0, S1​(λ)=1S_{1}(\lambda)=1, and

S2​n​(λ)=λ​Sn​(λ),S2​n+1​(λ)=Sn​(λ)+Sn+1​(λ).S_{2n}(\lambda)=\lambda S_{n}(\lambda),\quad S_{2n+1}(\lambda)=S_{n}(\lambda)+S_{n+1}(\lambda). (1.2)

The first 1616 terms of the sequence Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) are given in Table 1. This table suggests many patterns, several of which are recorded in Proposition 1.

While there are several papers which analyze the sequence Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) (see [3, 4, 5, 17] and the references therein), not much is known about the zeros of Stern polynomials. Because S2​n​(λ)=λ​Sn​(λ)S_{2n}(\lambda)=\lambda S_{n}(\lambda) for all n≥1n\geq 1, it suffices to examine the roots of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) only when nn is odd. Define

𝒮≔{z∈ℂ:Sn​(z)=0​ for some odd ​n≥1}.\mathcal{S}\coloneqq\{z\in\mathbb{C}:S_{n}(z)=0\text{ for some odd }n\geq 1\}.

In [5, Theorem 2.1], Gawron proves that 00, −1{-}1, −12{-}\tfrac{1}{2}, and −13-\tfrac{1}{3} are the only rational zeros of any Stern polynomial by showing, more generally, that any real number in the closed interval [−14,14][-\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{4}] cannot be in 𝒮\mathcal{S}. His methods extend easily to show that any complex number zz with |z|≤14|z|\leq\tfrac{1}{4} cannot be in 𝒮\mathcal{S}. For completeness, we record the proof here.

Theorem 1.

If z∈𝒮z\in\mathcal{S}, then |z|>14|z|>\tfrac{1}{4}.

Proof.

Let zz be any complex number with |z|≤14|z|\leq\tfrac{1}{4}. Let bn≔|Sn​(z)|b_{n}\coloneqq|S_{n}(z)| for each positive integer nn. We show more strongly that

b2​n+1>12​max⁡{bn,bn+1}>0b_{2n+1}>\tfrac{1}{2}\max\{b_{n},b_{n+1}\}>0 (1.3)

for all n≥1n\geq 1.

The proof of (1.3) proceeds by induction on nn. The base case, n=1n=1, follows because

b3=|z+1|≥34>12=12​max​{1,|z|}=12​max​{b1,b2}.b_{3}=|z+1|\geq\tfrac{3}{4}>\tfrac{1}{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\max\{1,|z|\}=\tfrac{1}{2}\max\{b_{1},b_{2}\}.

There are two cases to consider. First assume n=2​kn=2k is even. Then

b4​k+1\displaystyle b_{4k+1} =|S4​k+1​(z)|=|S2​k+1​(z)+S2​k​(z)|\displaystyle=|S_{4k+1}(z)|=|S_{2k+1}(z)+S_{2k}(z)|
=|z​Sk​(z)+S2​k+1​(z)|≥b2​k+1−14​bk\displaystyle=|zS_{k}(z)+S_{2k+1}(z)|\geq b_{2k+1}-\tfrac{1}{4}b_{k}
≥b2​k+1−12​b2​k+1=12​b2​k+1.\displaystyle\geq b_{2k+1}-\tfrac{1}{2}b_{2k+1}=\tfrac{1}{2}b_{2k+1}.

Moreover, b2​k+1≥12​bkb_{2k+1}\geq\frac{1}{2}b_{k}, and thus max⁡{b2​k,b2​k+1}=b2​k+1>0\max\{b_{2k},b_{2k+1}\}=b_{2k+1}>0. In this case, our inequality is proved.

Now assume n=2​k+1n=2k+1 is odd. Then

b4​k+3\displaystyle b_{4k+3} =|S4​k+3​(z)|=|S2​k+1​(z)+S2​k+2​(z)|\displaystyle=|S_{4k+3}(z)|=|S_{2k+1}(z)+S_{2k+2}(z)|
=|S2​k+1​(z)+z​Sk+1​(z)|≥b2​k+1−14​bk+1\displaystyle=|S_{2k+1}(z)+zS_{k+1}(z)|\geq b_{2k+1}-\frac{1}{4}b_{k+1}
≥b2​k+1−12​b2​k+1=12​b2​k+1.\displaystyle\geq b_{2k+1}-\tfrac{1}{2}b_{2k+1}=\tfrac{1}{2}b_{2k+1}.

Moreover, b2​k+1≥12​bk+1b_{2k+1}\geq\frac{1}{2}b_{k+1}, and so in this case we also have max⁡{b2​k,b2​k+1}=b2​k+1>0\max\{b_{2k},b_{2k+1}\}=b_{2k+1}>0. We have exhausted both cases, completing the proof of Theorem 1. ∎

In [3], Dilcher et. al. focus more specifically on the complex roots of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda). Their paper makes the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.

All elements of 𝒮\mathcal{S} lie in the half-plane {Rew<1}\{\operatorname{Re}w<1\}.

By generalizing the Enestrom-Kakeya theorem, they prove Conjecture 1 for several classes of positive integers nn taking the form 2n±k2^{n}\pm k, where kk is fixed and 2n≥k2^{n}\geq k. These are the only two papers the author could find which discuss the complex zeros of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda).

Figure 1 shows a snapshot of 𝒮\mathcal{S}. One striking feature of this figure is the contrasting behavior of these roots within the half-planes {Rew≥0}\{\operatorname{Re}w\geq 0\} and {Rew<0}\{\operatorname{Re}w<0\}. These differences present difficulties in fully characterizing the geometry of 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

In this paper, we partially resolve Conjecture 1 by establishing the following result.

Theorem 2.

All roots of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) lie outside the disk {|z−2|≤1}⊆ℂ\{\left|z-2\right|\leq 1\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}.

To prove Theorem 2, we use a continued fraction representation for a ratio of Stern polynomials (Theorem 3) independently discovered by Reznick [12] and Schinzel [13]. This allows us to use the Parabola Theorem (Theorem 4) to show that, for certain values of z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}, the denominators of these continued fractions can never be zero. Along the way, we establish inequalities in ℂ\mathbb{C} relating to the sums 1+z+⋯+zn−11+z+\cdots+z^{n-1} which may be of independent interest. The most notable of these inequalities is Theorems 7, which proves a lower bound for this geometric series whenever Re⁡z≥1\operatorname{Re}z\geq 1.

As a corollary, we obtain the following surprising fact, resolving a conjecture of Ulas and Ulas ([17]).

Corollary 1.

For each prime number pp, the Stern polynomial Sp​(λ)S_{p}(\lambda) is irreducible in ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

Ulas and Ulas had verified this conjecture computationally for the first million primes pp. Additionally, Schinzel in [14] proved Corollary 1 for all primes p<2017p<2017 by using finite differences to bound the leading coefficient of any proper divisor of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda). However, these previous attempts to prove the conjecture were algebraic in nature, whereas our proof depends on the analytic properties of 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

2 Stern Polynomial Preliminaries

Notation.

Write ℂ\mathbb{C} as usual for the field of complex numbers, and let ℂ^≔ℂ∪{∞}\hat{\mathbb{C}}\coloneqq\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\} be the extended complex plane. For all positive integers nn, we introduce the (non-standard) notation

(λ)n≔1+λ+⋯+λn−1=λn−1λ−1∈ℤ⁡[λ].(\lambda)_{n}\coloneqq 1+\lambda+\cdots+\lambda^{n-1}=\frac{\lambda^{n}-1}{\lambda-1}\in\mathbb{Z}[\lambda].

For continuity purposes, we set (1)n=n(1)_{n}=n. For any set S⊆ℂS\subseteq\mathbb{C}, define the auxiliary sets S+S^{+} and S−S^{-} via

S+≔S∩{Imw≥0}andS−≔S∩{Imw≤0}.S^{+}\coloneqq S\cap\{\operatorname{Im}w\geq 0\}\quad\text{and}\quad S^{-}\coloneqq S\cap\{\operatorname{Im}w\leq 0\}.

Furthermore, for U⊆ℂ^U\subseteq\hat{\mathbb{C}}, set U−1≔{w−1:w∈U}⊆ℂ^U^{-1}\coloneqq\{w^{-1}:w\in U\}\subseteq\hat{\mathbb{C}}. Finally, for all z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} and r≥0r\geq 0, let Br​(z)B_{r}(z) be the open Euclidean ball centered at zz with radius rr, and let Br​[z]B_{r}[z] denote the closed Euclidean ball centered at zz with radius rr.

We begin by recording some basic properties of the Stern polynomials. All of these can be proven by induction.

Proposition 1.

Let nn be a nonnegative integer.

  1. 1.

    Sn​(0)=0S_{n}(0)=0 when nn is even, and Sn​(0)=1S_{n}(0)=1 when nn is odd.

  2. 2.

    Sn​(1)=snS_{n}(1)=s_{n}, where sns_{n} is the Stern sequence (1.1).

  3. 3.

    Sn​(2)=nS_{n}(2)=n.

  4. 4.

    When n=2rn=2^{r} for a nonnegative integer rr, Sn​(λ)=λrS_{n}(\lambda)=\lambda^{r}.

  5. 5.

    When n=2r−1n=2^{r}-1 for a nonnegative integer rr, Sn​(λ)=(λ)rS_{n}(\lambda)=(\lambda)_{r}.

One of the most fundamental properties of the Stern sequence is the recursion

s2k​m+r=s2k−r​sm+sr​sm+1,s_{2^{k}m+r}=s_{2^{k}-r}s_{m}+s_{r}s_{m+1},

valid for m≥0m\geq 0 and 2k>r≥02^{k}>r\geq 0. The Stern polynomials satisfy an analogous recursion.

Proposition 2 ([13, Lemma 1]).

For all integers m≥0m\geq 0 and 2k>r≥02^{k}>r\geq 0,

S2k​m+r​(λ)=S2k−r​(λ)​Sm​(λ)+Sr​(λ)​Sm+1​(λ).S_{2^{k}m+r}(\lambda)=S_{2^{k}-r}(\lambda)S_{m}(\lambda)+S_{r}(\lambda)S_{m+1}(\lambda).
Corollary 2.

For positive integers aa and bb,

S2a+b−2b+1​(λ)=(λ)a​(λ)b+λa.S_{2^{a+b}-2^{b}+1}(\lambda)=(\lambda)_{a}(\lambda)_{b}+\lambda^{a}.
Proof.

Write 2a+b−2b+1=2b​(2a−1)+12^{a+b}-2^{b}+1=2^{b}(2^{a}-1)+1. Apply Proposition 2 with k=bk=b, m=2a−1m=2^{a}-1, and r=1r=1 to obtain

S2a+b−2b+1​(λ)\displaystyle S_{2^{a+b}-2^{b}+1}(\lambda) =S2b−1​(λ)​S2a−1​(λ)+S1​(λ)​S2a​(λ)\displaystyle=S_{2^{b}-1}(\lambda)S_{2^{a}-1}(\lambda)+S_{1}(\lambda)S_{2^{a}}(\lambda)
=(λ)b​(λ)a+λa.∎\displaystyle=(\lambda)_{b}(\lambda)_{a}+\lambda^{a}.\qed

Proposition 2 may be restated in a form that highlights its underlying structure. Note that any odd integer can be expressed in the form

[[a1,⋯,at]]:=2a1+⋯+at−2a2+⋯+at+⋯+(−1)t−1​2at+(−1)t,[[a_{1},\cdots,a_{t}]]:=2^{a_{1}+\cdots+a_{t}}-2^{a_{2}+\cdots+a_{t}}+\cdots+(-1)^{t-1}2^{a_{t}}+(-1)^{t}, (2.1)

where a1,…,ata_{1},\ldots,a_{t} are positive integers. For example, 2a+b−2b+1=[[a,b]]2^{a+b}-2^{b}+1=[[a,b]], so Corollary 2 takes the form

S[[a,b]]​(λ)=(λ)a​(λ)b+λa.S_{[[a,b]]}(\lambda)=(\lambda)_{a}(\lambda)_{b}+\lambda^{a}. (2.2)

[[a1,…,at−1,at]]\displaystyle[[a_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1},a_{t}]] =2a1+⋯+at−[[a2,…,at]]\displaystyle=2^{a_{1}+\cdots+a_{t}}-[[a_{2},\ldots,a_{t}]] (2.3)
=2at​[[a1,…,at−1]]+(−1)t.\displaystyle=2^{a_{t}}[[a_{1},\ldots,a_{t-1}]]+(-1)^{t}. (2.4)

For all sequences of positive integers a1a_{1}, …\ldots, ata_{t},

S[[a1,…,at]]​(λ)=(λ)a1​S[[a2,…,at]]​(λ)+λa1​S[[a3,…,at]]​(λ).S_{[[a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}]]}(\lambda)=(\lambda)_{a_{1}}S_{[[a_{2},\ldots,a_{t}]]}(\lambda)+\lambda^{a_{1}}S_{[[a_{3},\ldots,a_{t}]]}(\lambda). (2.5)

n\displaystyle n =[[a1,…,at]],\displaystyle=[[a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}]],
n′\displaystyle n^{\prime} =[[a2,…,at]],and\displaystyle=[[a_{2},\ldots,a_{t}]],\quad\text{and}

n=2r−n′=2r−(2r−a1−n′′)=2r−a1​(2a1−1)+n′′.n=2^{r}-n^{\prime}=2^{r}-(2^{r-a_{1}}-n^{\prime\prime})=2^{r-a_{1}}(2^{a_{1}}-1)+n^{\prime\prime}.

Equation (2.5) bears similarities identities satisfied by continuants of continued fractions (see [7]). This suggests the Stern polynomials have a continued fraction representation in terms of the sequence aia_{i}, which we now state and prove.

Corollary 3 ([13, Theorem 1]).

Let a1,…,ata_{1},\ldots,a_{t} be positive integers, where t≥2t\geq 2. Then

S[[a1,…,at]]​(λ)S[[a2,…,at]]​(λ)=(λ)a1+λa1(λ)a2+λa2⋯+⋯(λ)at−1+λat−1(λ)at.\frac{S_{[[a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}]]}(\lambda)}{S_{[[a_{2},\ldots,a_{t}]]}(\lambda)}=(\lambda)_{a_{1}}+\cfrac{\lambda^{a_{1}}}{(\lambda)_{a_{2}}+\cfrac{\lambda^{a_{2}}}{\cdots+\cfrac{\cdots}{(\lambda)_{a_{t-1}}+\cfrac{\lambda^{a_{t-1}}}{(\lambda)_{a_{t}}}}}}\,. (2.6)
Proof.

Proceed by induction on tt. The base case t=2t=2 follows from (2.2) and the calculation

For the inductive step, apply Theorem 3. ∎

Corollary 3 will be the workhorse for our analysis of the roots of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda).

3 Continued Fractions and the Parabola Theorem

Recall that, for a complex number b0b_{0} and any finite sequences of complex numbers a1,…,ata_{1},\ldots,a_{t} and b1,…,btb_{1},\ldots,b_{t}, the (generalized) continued fraction b0+𝑲⁡(an|bn)b_{0}+\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|b_{n}) is the quotient

b0+𝑲⁡(an|bn)≔b0+a1b1+a2⋯+atbt.b_{0}+\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|b_{n})\coloneqq b_{0}+\cfrac{a_{1}}{b_{1}+\cfrac{a_{2}}{\cdots+\cfrac{a_{t}}{b_{t}}}}.

While continued fractions are most often studied in number theory, there has been significant study toward the convergence problem for generalized continued fractions – that is, determining sufficient conditions on (an)n=1∞(a_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty} and (bn)n=1∞(b_{n})_{n=1}^{\infty} for which the infinite continued fraction b0+𝑲⁡(an|bn)b_{0}+\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|b_{n}) converges in ℂ\mathbb{C}. In this regard, one may also consider a continued fraction as a sequence of fractional linear transformations

Sn=s0∘s1∘⋯∘sn,S_{n}=s_{0}\circ s_{1}\circ\cdots\circ s_{n}, (3.1)

where

s0​(w)≔b0+wandsn​(w)≔anbn+w.s_{0}(w)\coloneqq b_{0}+w\quad\text{and}\quad s_{n}(w)\coloneqq\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}+w}.

This connection between continued fractions and fractional linear transformations was first discovered by Weyl [18]. While we will not need convergence of continued fractions, we will borrow some of the techniques and theorems from this field. For a more detailed investigation, consult [9, Chapter 3] and the references therein.

One way to analyze a generalized continued fraction is to find an element set and a value set for this fraction. We present the definitions for these sets in the special case where bj=1b_{j}=1 for all jj; later, we will see that this presents no loss of generality.

Definition 1.

A set V⊂ℂ^V\subset\hat{\mathbb{C}} is a value set for 𝑲⁡(an|1)\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|1) if

an1+V⊆V​ for ​n=1,2,3,….\frac{a_{n}}{1+V}\subseteq V\text{ for }n=1,2,3,\ldots.
Definition 2.

For a given value set VV, the set E⊂ℂ^E\subset\hat{\mathbb{C}} given by

E≔{a∈ℂ:a1+V⊆V}E\coloneqq\left\{a\in\mathbb{C}\,{:}\,\frac{a}{1+V}\subseteq V\right\}

is called the element set corresponding to the value set VV.

Observe that if an∈Ea_{n}\in E for all nn, and 0∈V0\in V, then 𝑲⁡(an|1)=Sn​(0)∈V\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|1)=S_{n}(0)\in V for all n≥0n\geq 0. This allows us to bound 𝑲⁡(an|1)\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|1) in ℂ^\hat{\mathbb{C}} using geometric arguments that are more precise than those found through just the Triangle Inequality.

One may hope that, given an element set EE for a continued fraction, we may find a value set VV corresponding to EE. However, in most cases, this is a nearly impossible task. It is significantly easier to proceed in the opposite direction: fix a value set VV and find an element set EE corresponding to VV. There are many theorems in the literature which take this form. We state the most relevant result for us below.

Theorem 4 (Parabola Theorem, [9, Theorem 3.43]).

For fixed |α|<π2|\alpha|<\tfrac{\pi}{2}, let

Vα≔−12+ei​α​ℍ¯={w∈ℂ:Re⁡(w​e−i​α)≥−12​cos⁡α}V_{\alpha}\coloneqq-\tfrac{1}{2}+e^{i\alpha}\overline{\mathbb{H}}=\{w\in\mathbb{C}:\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\alpha})\geq-\tfrac{1}{2}\cos\alpha\}

and

Eα≔{a∈ℂ:|a|−Re⁡(a​e−2​i​α)≤12​cos2⁡α}.E_{\alpha}\coloneqq\{a\in\mathbb{C}:|a|-\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-2i\alpha})\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\cos^{2}\alpha\}.

Then EαE_{\alpha} is the element set for continued fractions 𝑲⁡(an|1)\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|1) corresponding to the value set VαV_{\alpha}.

The region VαV_{\alpha} is a half-plane whose boundary is a line intersecting the real axis at z=−12z=-\tfrac{1}{2}. In particular, because |α|<π2|\alpha|<\tfrac{\pi}{2}, VαV_{\alpha} contains the half-line [−12,∞)[-\tfrac{1}{2},\infty). The boundary of EαE_{\alpha} is a parabola with focus at the origin and vertex at −14​e2​i​α​cos2⁡α-\tfrac{1}{4}e^{2i\alpha}\cos^{2}\alpha. This parabola intersects the real axis at z=−14z=-\tfrac{1}{4}.

Remark 1.

Some sources include ∞\infty in the half-plane VαV_{\alpha}. However, because −1∉Vα-1\notin V_{\alpha}, we know a priori that Sn​(w)=an1+Sn−1​(w)S_{n}(w)=\tfrac{a_{n}}{1+S_{n-1}(w)} never equals ∞∈ℂ^\infty\in\hat{\mathbb{C}}. We choose to ignore ∞\infty to make the presentation cleaner.

We now tie the continued fraction theory back to Stern polynomials. Recall that Corollary 3 expresses the ratio of two Stern polynomials as a continued fraction with elements in ℂ\mathbb{C}. This form on its own is difficult to work with. We instead note (e.g. [9, Corollary 2.15]) that any continued fraction 𝑲⁡(an|bn)\boldsymbol{K}(a_{n}|b_{n}) with bj≠0b_{j}\neq 0 is equivalent to the continued fraction 𝑲⁡(cn|1)\boldsymbol{K}(c_{n}|1), where cj=ajbj​bj+1c_{j}=\tfrac{a_{j}}{b_{j}b_{j+1}}. As an explicit example,

S[[2,3,5]]​(λ)S[[3,5]]​(λ)=(λ)2+λ2(λ)3+λ3(λ)5=(λ)2​[1+λ2(λ)2​(λ)31+λ3(λ)3​(λ)5].\frac{S_{[[2,3,5]]}(\lambda)}{S_{[[3,5]]}(\lambda)}=(\lambda)_{2}+\cfrac{\lambda^{2}}{(\lambda)_{3}+\cfrac{\lambda^{3}}{(\lambda)_{5}}}=(\lambda)_{2}\left[1+\cfrac{\dfrac{\lambda^{2}}{(\lambda)_{2}(\lambda)_{3}}}{1+\cfrac{\lambda^{3}}{(\lambda)_{3}(\lambda)_{5}}}\right]. (3.2)
Remark 2.

While continued fractions of the form 𝑲⁡(1|dn)\boldsymbol{K}(1|d_{n}) are more common, the coefficients dnd_{n} are significantly messier than the coefficients cnc_{n} (see [9, Corollary 2.15]). We opt to use the less-common form 𝑲⁡(cn|1)\boldsymbol{K}(c_{n}|1) to simplify our analysis.

Equation (3.2) suggests that the ratios za(z)a​(z)b\tfrac{z^{a}}{(z)_{a}(z)_{b}}, where aa and bb are any positive integers, may play some importance. For this reason, we define za,b≔za(z)a​(z)bz_{a,b}\coloneqq\tfrac{z^{a}}{(z)_{a}(z)_{b}} and

𝒜z≔{za,b:(a,b)∈ℕ2}.\mathcal{A}_{z}\coloneqq\left\{z_{a,b}:(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}\right\}.

Suppose 𝒜z⊆Eα\mathcal{A}_{z}\subseteq E_{\alpha} for some angle α\alpha with |α|<π2|\alpha|<\tfrac{\pi}{2}. Then VαV_{\alpha} is a value set for the continued fraction (2.6) at λ=z\lambda=z. In particular, ∞\infty is not a possible value for this fraction, so Sn​(z)≠0S_{n}(z)\neq 0 for any zz.

Throughout the rest of the paper, we use α=π12\alpha=\tfrac{\pi}{12} in our applications of Theorem 4. In this case, Theorem 4 reduces to the following result.

Theorem 5.

Let EE denote the parabola

E≔Eπ/12\displaystyle E\coloneqq E_{\pi/12} ={a∈ℂ:|a|−Re(ae−πi/6)≤2+38}\displaystyle=\left\{a\in\mathbb{C}:|a|-\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-\pi i/6})\leq\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{8}\right\}
={x+y​i∈ℂ:x2+y2≤32​x+12​y+2+38}.\displaystyle=\left\{x+yi\in\mathbb{C}:\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\leq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{8}\right\}.

Suppose z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} is a complex number such that za,b∈Ez_{a,b}\in E for all (a,b)∈ℕ2(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{2}. Then zz is not a root of any Stern polynomial.

The remainder of this paper is dedicated to showing za,b∈Ez_{a,b}\in E whenever zz lies in the set

ℬ≔B1[2]={|w−2|≤1},\mathcal{B}\coloneqq B_{1}[2]=\{\left|w-2\right|\leq 1\},

thus proving Theorem 5. See Figure 2 for an example.

Let us see how Theorem 5 proves Theorem 1.

Proof (Theorem 1).

Suppose PP is a factor of some Stern polynomial with deg⁡P=d\deg P=d, and factor it over ℂ\mathbb{C}:

P⁡(λ)=1+c1​λ+⋯+cd​λd=cd​∏k=1d(λ−μk).P(\lambda)=1+c_{1}\lambda+\cdots+c_{d}\lambda^{d}=c_{d}\prod_{k=1}^{d}(\lambda-\mu_{k}).

Then P⁡(2)=cd​∏k=1d(2−μk)P(2)=c_{d}\prod_{k=1}^{d}(2-\mu_{k}). Because cd≥1c_{d}\geq 1 and |2−μk|>1|2-\mu_{k}|>1 by Theorem 5, it follows that P⁡(2)>1P(2)>1. Thus, if Sp​(λ)=P⁡(λ)​Q​(λ)S_{p}(\lambda)=P(\lambda)Q(\lambda) for non-constant PP and QQ in ℤ⁡[λ]\mathbb{Z}[\lambda], then

p=Sp​(2)=P⁡(2)​Q​(2).p=S_{p}(2)=P(2)Q(2).

This implies P⁡(2)=1P(2)=1 or Q⁡(2)=1Q(2)=1, which is impossible. ∎

4 A Potpourri of Complex Inequalities

This chapter is the main content of the paper. We prove several inequalities in ℂ\mathbb{C} needed for the main theorem. Some results tie directly into the Stern polynomials Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda), while others are independent results which seem interesting in their own rights.

4.1 Preliminaries

Here we list some inequalities which are not directly related to complex numbers but which will be used several times in the following three sections.

Our first inequality is a lower bound on sin⁡x\sin x. While it is not as tight as the Taylor inequality sin⁡x≥x−x36\sin x\geq x-\frac{x^{3}}{6} for small xx, it exhibits a second equality case at x=πx=\pi.

Proposition 3.

For all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R},

sin⁡x≥x−x2π.\sin x\geq x-\frac{x^{2}}{\pi}. (4.1)
Proof.

There are two cases to consider.

  • •

    First suppose x∈[0,π]x\in[0,\pi]. Because both sin⁡x\sin x and x−x2πx-\tfrac{x^{2}}{\pi} are symmetric about the axis x=π2x=\tfrac{\pi}{2}, it suffices to prove the inequality for x∈[0,π2]x\in[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}]. Within this smaller interval, cosine is concave down with cos⁡0=1\cos 0=1 and cos⁡π2=0\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}=0, so

    cos⁡x≥1−2​xπ.\cos x\geq 1-\frac{2x}{\pi}. (4.2)

    Integrating both sides of (4.2) yields (4.1) in this case.

  • •

    Now suppose x∉[0,π]x\notin[0,\pi]. By symmetry, it suffices to prove the inequality for x≥πx\geq\pi. In this interval, 1−2​xπ≤−1≤cos⁡x1-\tfrac{2x}{\pi}\leq-1\leq\cos x. It follows that (4.2), and thus (4.1), holds as well.

∎

We also need a variation of Bernoulli’s Inequality which lower bounds (1+x)r(1+x)^{r} by its second-order Taylor expansion. If r≥2r\geq 2 is a positive integer, then certainly

(1+x)r=∑j=0r(rj)​xj≥1+r​x+(r2)​x2whenever ​x≥0.(1+x)^{r}=\sum_{j=0}^{r}\binom{r}{j}x^{j}\geq 1+rx+\binom{r}{2}x^{2}\quad\text{whenever }x\geq 0. (4.3)

However, this argument does not work for general r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}, because the binomial coefficients (rj)\binom{r}{j} may be negative. Nevertheless, (4.3) still holds if rr is real. We present a proof using Taylor expansions. For a generalization of this inequality, consult [6].

Proposition 4.

For all x≥0x\geq 0 and real r≥2r\geq 2,

(1+x)r≥1+r​x+(r2)​x2.(1+x)^{r}\geq 1+rx+\binom{r}{2}x^{2}.
Proof.

Let f⁡(t)≔(1+t)rf(t)\coloneqq(1+t)^{r}. Observe that f′′′​(t)=r⁡(r−1)​(r−2)​(1+t)r−3f^{\prime\prime\prime}(t)=r(r-1)(r-2)(1+t)^{r-3} is nonnegative on (0,∞)(0,\infty). It follows from Taylor’s Theorem that

(1+x)r=1+r​x+(r2)​x2+∫0xf′′′​(t)6​(x−t)2​𝑑t≥1+r​x+(r2)​x2.∎(1+x)^{r}=1+rx+\binom{r}{2}x^{2}+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{f^{\prime\prime\prime}(t)}{6}(x-t)^{2}\,dt\geq 1+rx+\binom{r}{2}x^{2}.\qed

4.2 Bounding Geometric Series on {Rew≥1}\{\operatorname{Re}w\geq 1\}

The main technical difficulty in our analysis of the roots of Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) comes from estimating (z)n(z)_{n}. This is significantly more difficult than it seems, especially for complex numbers zz of the form 1+i​t1+it where tt is small. For example, it is tempting to write

|(z)n|=|zn−1z−1|≥|z|n−1|z−1|=(1+t2)n/2−1t.|(z)_{n}|=\left|\frac{z^{n}-1}{z-1}\right|\geq\frac{|z|^{n}-1}{|z-1|}=\frac{(1+t^{2})^{n/2}-1}{t}. (4.4)

However, the right hand side of (4.4) is n2​t+𝒪⁡(t2)\tfrac{n}{2}t+\mathcal{O}(t^{2}) as t→0t\to 0, whereas |(z)n||(z)_{n}| tends to nn as z→1z\to 1.

There seem to be few attempts to strengthen (4.4) in the literature. The most relevant result we could find is Problem 4795 in the American Mathematical Monthly, reproduced below. A proof appears in [11].

Theorem 6.

For all z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} with Re⁡z≥1\operatorname{Re}z\geq 1, and for all a≥1a\geq 1,

|(z)a|=|1+z+⋯+za−1|≥|z|a−1.|(z)_{a}|=|1+z+\cdots+z^{a-1}|\geq|z|^{a-1}.

This estimate will be useful later in this paper, but it still is not tight for z≈1z\approx 1. We now focus on finding a lower bound for |(z)n||(z)_{n}| that is tight near 11.

We first show that it suffices to lower bound |(z)n||(z)_{n}| on the line Re⁡w=1\operatorname{Re}w=1.

Lemma 1.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 be an integer, and suppose xx, x0x_{0}, and yy are real numbers with x≥x0≥1x\geq x_{0}\geq 1. Then

|(x+y​i)n|≥|(x0+y​i)n|.|(x+yi)_{n}|\geq|(x_{0}+yi)_{n}|.
Proof.

Both sides equal 11 when n=1n=1, so assume n≥2n\geq 2. Let z=x+y​iz=x+yi and z0≔x0+y​iz_{0}\coloneqq x_{0}+yi for ease of readability. Observe that

|(z)n|=|1+z+z2+⋯+zn−1|=∏j=1n−1|z−e2​π​i​j/n||(z)_{n}|=|1+z+z^{2}+\cdots+z^{n-1}|=\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}|z-e^{2\pi ij/n}|

and

|(z0)n|=|1+z0+z02+⋯+z0n−1|=∏j=1n−1|z0−e2​π​i​j/n|.|(z_{0})_{n}|=|1+z_{0}+z_{0}^{2}+\cdots+z_{0}^{n-1}|=\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}|z_{0}-e^{2\pi ij/n}|.

For each jj, because Re⁡(e2​π​i​j/n)≤1\operatorname{Re}(e^{2\pi ij/n})\leq 1 and x≥x0x\geq x_{0}, we have |z−e2​π​i​j/n|≥|z0−e2​π​i​j/n||z-e^{2\pi ij/n}|\geq|z_{0}-e^{2\pi ij/n}|. Multiplying all n−1n-1 such inequalities together yields

|1+z+z2+⋯+zn−1|≥|1+z0+z02+⋯+z0n−1|.∎|1+z+z^{2}+\cdots+z^{n-1}|\geq|1+z_{0}+z_{0}^{2}+\cdots+z_{0}^{n-1}|.\qed

We handle small values of nn numerically. Observe that (1+i​t)n(1+it)_{n} is a polynomial in tt, so

|(1+i​t)n|2\displaystyle|(1+it)_{n}|^{2} =(1+i​t)n​(1−i​t)n=(1+i​t)n−1i​t⋅(1−i​t)n−1−i​t\displaystyle=(1+it)_{n}(1-it)_{n}=\frac{(1+it)^{n}-1}{it}\cdot\frac{(1-it)^{n}-1}{-it}
=(1+t2)n−2​Re⁡(1+i​t)n+1t2\displaystyle=\frac{(1+t^{2})^{n}-2\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{n}+1}{t^{2}}

can be written in the form Pn​(t2)P_{n}(t^{2}) for some polynomial PnP_{n}. This means we may manually compute PnP_{n} for small nn and use standard calculus techniques to numerically bound their minima. These computations are shown in Table 2 for 1≤n≤141\leq n\leq 14.

Unfortunately, these explicit polynomials are hard to analyze for large nn. (In particular, observe that the sequence of minima is not monotonic, instead peaking at n=9n=9.) This means we need a fundamentally different approach to bound PnP_{n} in general.

The key estimate for us is the following inequality.

Theorem 7.

For all real numbers tt and all positive integers nn,

|(1+i​tn)n−1|≥|ei​t−1|=2​sin⁡t2.\left|\left(1+\frac{it}{n}\right)^{n}-1\right|\geq\big|e^{it}-1\big|=2\sin\frac{t}{2}. (4.5)

Carlo Beenakker conjectured Theorem 7 in response to a question by the author on MathOverflow [16], and Terence Tao later confirmed this conjecture in the same thread. To make this paper self-contained, and to record the proof of this inequality in print, we replicate Tao’s argument below with some modifications in exposition.

Proof (Tao, [16]).

The proof proceeds in four steps. The first step rewrites (4.5) into polar coordinate form to obtain the equivalent inequality (4.8). The next three steps prove (4.8) by performing casework on different ranges of tt.

|ei​t−1|=2​|sin⁡t2|≤2⋅|t|2=|t|.|e^{it}-1|=2\left|\sin\frac{t}{2}\right|\leq 2\cdot\frac{|t|}{2}=|t|. (4.6)

|(1+i​t2)2−1|=t2+(t24)2≥|t|≥|ei​t−1|,\left|\left(1+\frac{it}{2}\right)^{2}-1\right|=\sqrt{t^{2}+\left(\frac{t^{2}}{4}\right)^{2}}\geq|t|\geq|e^{it}-1|,

Without loss of generality assume t≥0t\geq 0. We may take advantage of the estimate (1+i​tn)n≈ei​t(1+\tfrac{it}{n})^{n}\approx e^{it} by writing (1+i​tn)n=r​ei⁡(t−ε)(1+\tfrac{it}{n})^{n}=re^{i(t-\varepsilon)}, where

r≔(1+t2n2)n/2andε≔t−n​arctan⁡tn.r\coloneqq\left(1+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}\right)^{n/2}\quad\text{and}\quad\varepsilon\coloneqq t-n\arctan\frac{t}{n}.

We expect that ε\varepsilon should be relatively small. Indeed, upon integrating the inequalities 1−x2≤11+x2≤11-x^{2}\leq\tfrac{1}{1+x^{2}}\leq 1 (true for all xx) we have x−x33≤arctan⁡x≤xx-\frac{x^{3}}{3}\leq\arctan x\leq x for all x≥0x\geq 0. It follows that

0≤ε≤t33​n2.0\leq\varepsilon\leq\frac{t^{3}}{3n^{2}}. (4.7)

To finish the setup, observe that squaring both sides of (4.5) yields the equivalent inequality

r2−2​r​cos⁡(t−ε)+1≥2−2​cos⁡t.r^{2}-2r\cos(t-\varepsilon)+1\geq 2-2\cos t.

This rearranges to

(r−1)2+2​(r−1)​(1−cos⁡(t−ε))≥2​(cos⁡(t−ε)−cos⁡t).(r-1)^{2}+2(r-1)\Big(1-\cos(t-\varepsilon)\Big)\geq 2\Big(\cos(t-\varepsilon)-\cos t\Big). (4.8)

Step 2: t>𝟖𝟑\boldsymbol{t>\tfrac{8}{3}}.

In this region, r−1r-1 is large enough that we expect the first term (r−1)2(r-1)^{2} to dominate on its own. By Bernoulli’s Inequality, we make the estimate

r−1=(1+t2n2)n/2−1≥n2⋅t2n2=t22​n.r-1=\left(1+\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}\right)^{n/2}-1\geq\frac{n}{2}\cdot\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}=\frac{t^{2}}{2n}.

cos⁡(t−ε)−cos⁡t≤ε≤t33​n2.\cos(t-\varepsilon)-\cos t\leq\varepsilon\leq\frac{t^{3}}{3n^{2}}.

It follows that (r−1)2≥2​(cos⁡(t−ε)−cos⁡t)(r-1)^{2}\geq 2(\cos(t-\varepsilon)-\cos t) when

Within this range, we instead show that the second term, namely 2​(r−1)​(1−cos⁡(t−ε))2(r-1)(1-\cos(t-\varepsilon)), dominates. Here, cos⁡t≤0\cos t\leq 0 and

1−cos⁡(t−ε)≥1−ε≥1−t33​n2.1-\cos(t-\varepsilon)\geq 1-\varepsilon\geq 1-\frac{t^{3}}{3n^{2}}.

2⋅n2⋅t2n2​(1−t33​n2)≥2​t33​n2,2\cdot\frac{n}{2}\cdot\frac{t^{2}}{n^{2}}\left(1-\frac{t^{3}}{3n^{2}}\right)\geq 2\frac{t^{3}}{3n^{2}},

23​t+t33​n2≤n.\frac{2}{3}t+\frac{t^{3}}{3n^{2}}\leq n.

23​t+t33​n2≤23⋅83+(8/3)33⋅32=1808729<3.\frac{2}{3}t+\frac{t^{3}}{3n^{2}}\leq\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{8}{3}+\frac{(8/3)^{3}}{3\cdot 3^{2}}=\frac{1808}{729}<3.

(r−1)2+2​(r−1)​(1−cos⁡t)≥2​r​(cos⁡(t−ε)−cos⁡t).(r-1)^{2}+2(r-1)(1-\cos t)\geq 2r\Big(\cos(t-\varepsilon)-\cos t\Big). (4.9)

1−cos⁡tsin⁡t=tan⁡t2≥t2.\frac{1-\cos t}{\sin t}=\tan\frac{t}{2}\geq\frac{t}{2}.

2​(r−1)​t2≥2​r​ε2(r-1)\frac{t}{2}\geq 2r\varepsilon

r≤(1+(π/2)2n2)n/2≤exp⁡((π/2)2n2​n2)=exp⁡(π28​n).r\leq\left(1+\frac{(\pi/2)^{2}}{n^{2}}\right)^{n/2}\leq\exp\left(\frac{(\pi/2)^{2}}{n^{2}}\frac{n}{2}\right)=\exp\left(\frac{\pi^{2}}{8n}\right).

exp⁡(π224)<exp⁡(12)=e<2<94,\exp\left(\frac{\pi^{2}}{24}\right)<\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\sqrt{e}<2<\frac{9}{4},

4.3 Bounding Geometric Series on ℬ\mathcal{B}

Recall that ℬ\mathcal{B} is the disk {|w−2|≤1}⊆ℂ\{|w-2|\leq 1\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}. While Theorem 7 is strong in its own right, it is not quite sufficient to show Theorem 1. We opt to establish a separate lower bound for |(w)n||(w)_{n}| when w∈ℬw\in\mathcal{B}. This bound is not the strongest possible (see the remark before Proposition 8), but it is sufficient for our purposes.

Theorem 8.

Let nn be a positive integer, and suppose z∈ℬz\in\mathcal{B}. Then |(z)n|≥min⁡(n,112)|(z)_{n}|\geq\min(n,\tfrac{11}{2}).

For all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and t∈(0,n​π]t\in(0,n\pi], let

wn,t≔2−ei​t/n¯=(2−cos⁡tn)+i​sin⁡tn.w_{n,t}\coloneqq\overline{2-e^{it/n}}=\left(2-\cos\frac{t}{n}\right)+i\sin\frac{t}{n}.

Just as in the proof of Theorem 7, we aim to take advantage of the approximation wn,t≈ei​tw_{n,t}\approx e^{it} for large nn. The next few propositions will establish several lower bounds for |(wn,t)n||(w_{n,t})_{n}|.

Proposition 5.

For integer n≥1n\geq 1 and real t≥0t\geq 0, we have

|wn,tn−1wn,t−1|≥n⁡(1−t2​π).\left|\frac{w_{n,t}^{n}-1}{w_{n,t}-1}\right|\geq n\left(1-\frac{t}{2\pi}\right).

|wn,tn−1wn,t−1|≥|(1+i​sin⁡tn)n−1(1+i​sin⁡tn)−1|=|(1+i​sin⁡tn)n−1|sin⁡tn.\left|\frac{w_{n,t}^{n}-1}{w_{n,t}-1}\right|\geq\left|\frac{(1+i\sin\frac{t}{n})^{n}-1}{(1+i\sin\frac{t}{n})-1}\right|=\frac{\left|(1+i\sin\frac{t}{n})^{n}-1\right|}{\sin\frac{t}{n}}.

Now write sin⁡tn=1n⋅n​sin⁡tn\sin\frac{t}{n}=\tfrac{1}{n}\cdot n\sin\tfrac{t}{n} and apply Lemma 7 to obtain

|(1+i​sin⁡tn)n−1|\displaystyle\left|\left(1+i\sin\frac{t}{n}\right)^{n}-1\right| =|(1+in⋅n​sin⁡tn)n−1|\displaystyle=\left|\left(1+\frac{i}{n}\cdot n\sin\frac{t}{n}\right)^{n}-1\right|
≥|ei​n​sin⁡tn−1|=2​sin⁡(n2​sin⁡tn).\displaystyle\geq\left|e^{in\sin\frac{t}{n}}-1\right|=2\sin\left(\frac{n}{2}\sin\frac{t}{n}\right).

|(1+i​sin⁡tn)n−1|sin⁡tn\displaystyle\frac{\left|(1+i\sin\frac{t}{n})^{n}-1\right|}{\sin\frac{t}{n}} ≥2​sin⁡(n2​sin⁡tn)sin⁡tn=n⋅sin⁡(n2​sin⁡tn)n2​sin⁡tn\displaystyle\geq\frac{2\sin(\frac{n}{2}\sin\frac{t}{n})}{\sin\frac{t}{n}}=n\cdot\frac{\sin(\frac{n}{2}\sin\frac{t}{n})}{\frac{n}{2}\sin\frac{t}{n}}
≥n⁡(1−n2​sin⁡tnπ)≥n⁡(1−t2​π).∎\displaystyle\geq n\left(1-\frac{\frac{n}{2}\sin\frac{t}{n}}{\pi}\right)\geq n\left(1-\frac{t}{2\pi}\right).\qed

The second bound concerns values of tt away from 00.

Proposition 6.

For all n≥4n\geq 4 and t≥0t\geq 0, we have

|wn,tn−1wn,t−1|≥2​n​sin⁡t2​n.\left|\frac{w_{n,t}^{n}-1}{w_{n,t}-1}\right|\geq 2n\sin\frac{t}{2n}.
Proof.

Because wn,t=(2−cos⁡tn)+i​sin⁡tnw_{n,t}=(2-\cos\tfrac{t}{n})+i\sin\tfrac{t}{n}, compute

|wn|2\displaystyle\left|w_{n}\right|^{2} =(2−cos⁡tn)2+sin2⁡tn\displaystyle=\left(2-\cos\frac{t}{n}\right)^{2}+\sin^{2}\frac{t}{n}
=5−4​cos⁡tn=1+8​sin2⁡t2​n.\displaystyle=5-4\cos\frac{t}{n}=1+8\sin^{2}\frac{t}{2n}.

It follows by the Triangle Inequality and sin⁡x≥x−x36\sin x\geq x-\tfrac{x^{3}}{6} that

|wn,tn−1wn,t−1|\displaystyle\left|\frac{w_{n,t}^{n}-1}{w_{n,t}-1}\right| ≥|wn,t|n−1|wn,t−1|=(1+8​sin2⁡t2​n)n/2−12​sin⁡t2​n.\displaystyle\geq\frac{\left|w_{n,t}\right|^{n}-1}{\left|w_{n,t}-1\right|}=\frac{(1+8\sin^{2}\frac{t}{2n})^{n/2}-1}{2\sin\frac{t}{2n}}.

Our third inequality is a slight tightening of Proposition 6 as t→0t\to 0.

Proposition 7.

6 Comments and Future Work

Because the sequence Sn​(λ)S_{n}(\lambda) is relatively new, several unresolved questions regarding their properties and zero distributions persist. These questions touch many areas of mathematics, including continued fraction theory and combinatorics.

While Theorem 4 was sufficient to show ℬ\mathcal{B} has no Stern zeros, it cannot be used to show that all Stern zeros have real part less than 11. There exist complex numbers zz with Re⁡z≥1\operatorname{Re}z\geq 1 for which the set 𝒜z\mathcal{A}_{z} is not a subset of any parabolic region EαE_{\alpha}. Figure 6 illustrates z=1+2.5​iz=1+2.5i as an example. Any attempts to prove this stronger conjecture will need more general results from continued fraction theory.

Stronger estimates for |(z)m||(z)_{m}| would also be desirable. For example, it may be possible to strengthen Lemma 1 to a statement of the form

|(x+y​i)n|≥C​|(x0+y​i)n|,|(x+yi)_{n}|\geq C|(x_{0}+yi)_{n}|,

where C=Cn,y,x,x0C=C_{n,y,x,x_{0}} is a positive number greater than 11. We hope that this stronger statement may lead to cleaner proofs and further generalizations of Theorem 8.

Finally, let us comment on a remark from the introduction of this paper. In Section 1, we mentioned the stark contrast in the behavior of 𝒮\mathcal{S} between the two half-planes {Rew>0}\{\operatorname{Re}w>0\} and {Rew<0}\{\operatorname{Re}w<0\}. Recent papers have aimed to make these differences explicit. For example, while we conjecture that the set {Re⁡w:w∈𝒮}\{\operatorname{Re}w:w\in\mathcal{S}\} is bounded above, it is not bounded below.

Theorem 9 ([3, Proposition 3.3]).

The roots of Sαn​(λ)S_{\alpha_{n}}(\lambda), where αn=13​(2n−(−1)n)\alpha_{n}=\tfrac{1}{3}(2^{n}-(-1)^{n}), are negative real numbers of the form

−14​sec2⁡(j​πn),j=1,2,…,⌊n−12⌋.-\frac{1}{4}\sec^{2}\left(\frac{j\pi}{n}\right),\quad j=1,2,\ldots,\lfloor\tfrac{n-1}{2}\rfloor.

Consequently, the interval (−∞,−14](-\infty,-\tfrac{1}{4}] is dense in 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

This leads into a related question: is the set of imaginary parts bounded? Surprisingly, the answer is also “no”.

Theorem 10.

The polynomials Stn​(λ)S_{t_{n}}(\lambda), where

tn=4n+1+(−2)n+13,t_{n}=\frac{4^{n+1}+(-2)^{n}+1}{3},

have roots zn∈ℂz_{n}\in\mathbb{C} satisfying Im⁡zn→∞\operatorname{Im}z_{n}\to\infty as n→∞n\to\infty.

The proof begins by finding a closed form for Stn​(λ)S_{t_{n}}(\lambda) (involving the principal square root in ℂ\mathbb{C}), then uses Rouché’s Theorem along with careful asymptotics to show there exist roots with arbitrarily large imaginary part. The interested reader may consult the author’s doctoral thesis [1] for the details. The author believes Re⁡zn≍(Im⁡zn)2\operatorname{Re}z_{n}\asymp(\operatorname{Im}z_{n})^{2}, but has not worked out the details.
